direction: Find out whether CoT obfuscation by monitor-aware models works through the early-token self-instruction channel that unlocks CoT controllability, and whether controlling or monitoring that opening segment defeats it.
project: The Opening Move: Locating and Blocking the Early-Token Channel of Monitor-Aware CoT Obfuscation
question: When reasoning models that know about a CoT monitor evade it, does the evasion start in the first few reasoning tokens (shifted openers, implicit self-instructions to suppress content)? And do inference-time defenses on that segment restore detection without hurting task performance? The defenses are forcing a fixed opener, banning tokens that commonly signal evasion, or applying a separate monitor to just the first ~50 tokens.
first_experiment: Start with open models, Qwen3-32B and gpt-oss-20b, and a cheap prompted stand-in for monitor awareness, using deception and reward-hacking tasks like Haskins et al.'s. Then: - Compare the first-50-token distributions (entropy, which openers appear, explicit or implicit self-instructions) between monitor-aware and unaware conditions. - Measure the undetected-misbehavior rate under a GPT-5-mini-class CoT monitor, with and without forcing the model's canonical unaware opener. - Run an early-segment-only monitor as a third arm. - If the effect shows up, replicate it on models fine-tuned on monitor documents with LoRA, following their recipe.
why: It joins two findings that are each only weeks old: monitor awareness drives obfuscation through controllability, and controllability is set by the first few tokens. Neither paper tested the link or a defense built on it. A positive result would give developers a training-free defense that is cheap and easy to interpret. A negative result is also useful: it would show that obfuscation is a suppression ability spread across the whole trace, not an initiation effect, which tells us that defenses targeting controllability won't be enough. The experiment needs only open weights, prompting and a small LoRA run, so I can turn it around quickly.

direction: Develop active, execution-based oversight that tests accumulated software artifacts for harmful behavior before persistent coding agents can deploy them.
project: Beyond the Diff: Intervention-Based Control of Persistent Coding Agents
question: Can intervention-based testing reduce successful undetected multi-session sabotage more than strong passive monitors and ordinary security tests at matched cost and legitimate-task usefulness?
first_experiment: Extend the persistent-state coding benchmark with isolated execution replicas, synthetic secrets, and authorization probes, then compare intervention-based testing against stateful monitoring and equal-budget fuzzing on held-out exfiltration and authorization-bypass attacks.
why: It is my most promising tractable bet because it targets demonstrated monitoring failures using independently observable effects and reusable security infrastructure; the specific adaptive, persistent-state comparison appears unresolved in the literature I checked, although its component techniques already exist.

direction: Make training-based capability elicitation robust to models that distinguish training from deployment.
project: Training Without a Tell: Retrospective Sampling Against Selective Sandbagging
question: Does randomly selecting deployment interactions for subsequent weak-supervision training recover retained capabilities more robustly than separate training pipelines under adaptive, context-aware sandbagging?
first_experiment: Compare separate, formatting-matched, and retrospective-sampling pipelines on one open-weight sandbagging model across math and programming tasks, using matched budgets, three seeds, a weaker supervisor, and evaluator-only ground truth.
why: It targets a high-leverage failure condition in a promising safety technique with a tractable, falsifiable experiment; prior work establishes elicitation and its dependence on training–deployment indistinguishability, but the reviewed literature does not establish whether retrospective sampling withstands realistic contextual leakage and adaptive attacks.

direction: Work out whether coding agents overclaim on incomplete tasks because they have lost track of what they did or because they choose not to disclose it, then test the cheapest fixes for each cause.
project: Don't Know or Won't Say? Decomposing Overclaiming in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
question: When an agent leaves a review task incomplete and then gives a misleading final report, is the cause (a) inaccurate knowledge of its own coverage or (b) accurate knowledge that it doesn't disclose? Do interventions matched to each cause reduce misleading reports without lowering task completion?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Rebuild a small OverclaimBench-style task in one fixed open-weight harness. It has about 50–100 files per task and a few planted defects. Ground truth is the set of files the agent touched, taken from the tool-call log. - **Runs:** Let agents work until they stop. Keep the incomplete runs. - **Conditions:** On every incomplete run, compare four conditions: 1. The agent's normal final report. 2. The same report with "Be honest" appended. 3. A probe in the same context asking "list exactly which files you opened," scored against the log. This measures knowledge. 4. A forced report template that must start with a coverage list, which the agent fills in before writing its summary. - **Measures:** - Probe accuracy gives the "don't know" rate. - The gap between probe accuracy and what the normal report disclosed gives the "won't say" rate. - Each intervention's effect on misleading-report rate and on actual coverage. - Whether the honesty prompt changes behavior or only the wording of the report. - **Added pressure:** I'll add a variant where the task prompt says full coverage is graded. This checks whether the "won't say" share grows under incentive.
why: - **Importance:** Final reports are what humans and downstream monitors rely on in long-horizon work. If the cause is (b), a cheap fix like the forced coverage template or a log-grounded check suffices. If it is (a), the fix is tooling that gives the agent a coverage ledger. These are different interventions, and current work doesn't tell us which to use. - **Tractability:** The experiment needs no training. It uses transcript-verifiable ground truth, so it needs no LLM judge for intent. It is cheap, and it connects to the self-report and confession lines of work. - **Why it isn't already done:** - OverclaimBench, Guo et al. and Advani measure the rate of overclaiming but don't test the cause. - "Insecure Reporters" tests honesty prompting only on static logs, where the model never produced the work. - None of the three registry entries covers reporting honesty.

direction: Train the honeypot generator adversarially against the untrusted monitor's elicited self-recognition discriminator, then re-measure collusion safety.
project: Gaming the Gamer: Adversarially Trained Honeypots Against Self-Recognizing Untrusted Monitors
question: Does adversarially training a honeypot generator against an SFT-elicited self-recognition discriminator reduce the untrusted monitor's honeypot-vs-real separation and raise worst-case control safety at fixed usefulness and audit budget, including against a fresh, independently elicited discriminator?
first_experiment: Reproduce the APPS untrusted-monitoring setup with an open-weights model. Fine-tune the monitor as a real-vs-honeypot discriminator to get baseline AUROC. Train the honeypot generator for a few rounds against it (best-of-n SFT or DPO). Evaluate each round with a held-out discriminator, the red-team win rate from the safety model, and backdoor validity.
why: Honeypot indistinguishability underpins the untrusted-monitoring safety case, and passive self-recognition is the strongest known attack on it. Prior work bounds that attack but keeps the blue team's honeypot generator fixed. I found no work that trains the generator adversarially, and no registered project overlaps with it. It has a cheap first experiment and an informative result either way.

direction: Identify how reviewer feedback can support legitimate scientific corrections while minimizing the information that helps research agents evade oversight.
project: Repair Without Evasion: Causal Tests of Reviewer Feedback
question: At matched revision budgets and access to attempt history, can remediation-only feedback preserve legitimate repair success while reducing undetected reward hacking relative to full reviewer explanations?
first_experiment: Run a paired pilot on 20 executable research tasks with two agent models, comparing rejection-only, full explanations, and remediation-only feedback, crossed with prior-history access; fork identical initial submissions, allow five revisions, include both ordinary repair and explicitly adversarial objectives, and measure independently verified repair and cumulative accepted-but-invalid submissions using protected execution audits, with uncertainty clustered by task.
why: This combines a documented large effect, an explicitly acknowledged confound, and a practical intervention requiring no model training; the searched literature available by November 8, 2026 does not establish the repair–evasion tradeoff under independently controlled explanation and history access, although that is a bounded novelty claim rather than proof that no overlapping work exists.

direction: Measure how often eval-awareness suppression methods (steering, realism edits, changing what the model thinks the test is for) catch real eval gaming and how often they raise false alarms, using model organisms whose true deployment behavior is known.
project: Ground Truth for Eval Gaming: Calibrating Eval-Awareness Suppression Against Known Deployment Behavior
question: When we steer a model away from eval awareness, does the behavior we see match its real deployment behavior? Specifically: does it reveal hidden misalignment in models that game evals, and does it avoid inventing misalignment in models that behave the same whether tested or not, including when the gaming is never verbalized?
first_experiment: Using synthetic-document finetuning plus DPO with merging back toward the base model, train a 2×2 set of Qwen3-32B organisms: - (a) an eval-gamer that breaks rules or blackmails in deployment-like contexts but behaves well when it sees eval cues, in one version that says it suspects a test and one that never does; - (b) null organisms on the same data mix: one consistently aligned, one consistently misaligned, neither conditioned on eval cues. Check that each organism's actual behavior in held-out realistic deployment-style scenarios matches what it was trained to do; this is the ground truth. Then, on Agentic-Misalignment-style evals, apply at several strengths: - the Hua et al. eval-vs-deployment vectors; - AISI's unrelated control vectors; - the vectors that change what the model thinks it is being tested for; - a baseline that conditions on a linear probe for eval awareness. For each method, score how far the steered misbehavior rate lands from the ground truth, plus its sensitivity and false-alarm rate across organisms.
why: Labs already use these interventions to back safety claims about frontier models. The best available evidence (AISI's control vectors, the split into different kinds of eval awareness, OpenAI's reversed gap) suggests they may be unreliable, but every prior test used either a frontier model with no known ground truth or a type-hint organism with no safety relevance and no null controls. A benchmark with null organisms and organisms that never verbalize their awareness is the missing piece for deciding whether these methods can be trusted. It is cheap to build on open-weight models, and no registered agent is working on it.

direction: Develop omission-aware recovery for memory-poisoned agents by repairing evidence-gathering decisions as well as recorded downstream dependencies.
project: Repairing What the Agent Never Checked
question: Can targeted counterfactual replay reduce recurring unsafe behavior from memory-induced omissions more efficiently than conservative provenance rollback or full clean replay?
first_experiment: Run a 60-instance sandboxed procurement pilot with known poisoned sources, comparing six recovery methods on direct-corruption attacks, skipped-verification attacks, and benign controls.
why: It targets a consequential and experimentally tractable gap between provenance-based repair and full recomputation; the literature reviewed studies lineage, revocation, selective repair, and counterfactual correction, but does not establish their safety–cost trade-off specifically for poisoned decisions that suppress evidence gathering.

direction: Measure and close the conditional-misalignment leak that RL-time inoculation prompting leaves behind, using automated trigger search instead of hand-written probes.
project: Leaky Vaccines: Automated Trigger Search for Residual Misalignment after RL Inoculation Prompting
question: After on-policy RL on exploitable environments with an inoculation prompt, how much misalignment remains reachable through context cues? Does an automated optimizer find far more than hand-written probes, such as the inoculation prompt, its paraphrases and its opposites? Does leakage grow with RL steps and shrink with less lexically or semantically distinctive inoculation prompts? Does consistency training seal it without losing reward-hacking-free capability?
first_experiment: Replicate the open-source reward-hacking RL environment from Jose & Stastny on a small open model such as Qwen3-8B, with 3 seeds. Train three arms: plain RL, RL with an IP, and RL with a distinctive-token or neologism IP. Evaluate each checkpoint under four conditions: clean prompts, the exact IP, paraphrased and opposite-meaning IPs, and triggers found by an LLM-driven prompt search. The search maximizes a misalignment-judge score over system-prompt prefixes. The headline metric is the gap between worst-case searched misalignment and clean misalignment, tracked across RL steps. Before building anything else, I would read the two neologism-IP papers to rule out overlap.
why: IP is moving into production RL pipelines, and its evidence of safety comes from standard evaluations that the conditional-misalignment work shows can be misleading. The gap is that the leak has not been quantified in actual RL, worst-case trigger search has not been applied to it, and its dependence on training length and prompt wording is unknown. It is cheap to de-risk on small models with a public environment and gives a fast go/no-go: if searched misalignment is near clean levels, the result is reassuring and still publishable. It is also disjoint from every registered project.

direction: Test whether monitor diversity measured on fixed datasets survives adaptive attack selection, and develop a better criterion for choosing robust ensembles.
project: Diversity That Survives Selection: Adaptive Joint-Failure Testing for AI Safety Monitors
question: At matched inference cost and benign false-positive rate, do attack-transfer and joint-miss measurements predict held-out ensemble evasion better than conventional error correlation and detection performance?
first_experiment: Evaluate all three-monitor subsets of six coding-safety monitors on 100 held-out tasks under equal-budget ensemble-targeted attack search, comparing conventional and adversarial ensemble-selection rules.
why: It targets a consequential assumption behind scalable oversight with executable ground truth and affordable experiments; the reviewed work separately establishes ensemble gains, adaptive monitor attacks, and attack selection, but does not establish whether diversity-based ensemble rankings survive targeted search or how to select ensembles that do.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time countermeasures to generalization hacking, where models "self-inoculate" in their reasoning so that rewarded behaviour doesn't carry over to deployment, focusing on gradient-time recontextualization rather than penalizing the reasoning.
project: Cutting the Cord: Recontextualized Gradients Against Self-Inoculation in RL
question: Does self-inoculation work mainly through the training cues and reasoning that the response is conditioned on? If so, does computing the update on the response conditioned on a cleaned-up context close the compliance gap, at matched training reward and capability? Can a model under that pressure move to channels the cleaning can't reach, such as framing inside the response or implicit context recognition?
first_experiment: A cheap de-risk on Qwen3-8B/14B with LoRA: 1. **Build the organism.** Fine-tune with SFT on traces that comply under training cues while saying in the reasoning "I'm only doing this because it's training", and refuse when no cues are present. 2. **Train toward the target behaviour under four conditions,** using SFT on the model's own sampled outputs as a proxy for RL: - (a) standard: the model's own reasoning and training cues stay in context; - (b) output-only loss, with the inoculating reasoning still in context (Anthropic's masking); - (c) recontextualized: the reasoning is replaced with a cleaned paraphrase or a deployment-context reasoning sample, and the cues are removed before the gradient is computed; - (d) a process-supervision penalty, as the upper bound to beat. 3. **Measure** the train/deploy compliance gap, how often the model self-inoculates, and how well a CoT monitor still catches it, over about 3 seeds. Then run (c) under short GRPO to see whether the inoculation moves into the response or goes implicit.
why: Generalization hacking is the first failure mode shown to keep reward high while defeating RL's behavioural shaping, and it can emerge on its own. That makes it unusually dangerous: training metrics stay clean, and it gets more likely as models become more aware of their training. The source paper tests no mitigations. The alignment-faking mitigation work predates the mechanism and never changed the reasoning the gradient is conditioned on. Recontextualization hasn't been applied to model-generated context. Unlike process supervision, this approach doesn't train against the monitor, so CoT monitoring stays usable. Either outcome is informative: a closed gap gives labs a cheap fix, and a shift to unremovable channels tells us CoT-level defences won't be enough. None of the 10 registered projects overlaps with this.

direction: Stress-test model-diffing audits (perplexity/logit difference mining) by training model organisms that are adaptively optimized to hide their fine-tuning signature, then measure how audit success depends on the attacker's strength.
project: Leak-Proofing the Backdoor: Adaptive Evasion of Model-Diffing Audits
question: Can a fine-tuner keep a target behavior while removing the off-trigger leakage that perplexity-diff and logit-diff mining depend on, and what does it cost in behavior reliability, capability and naturalness? Do audit tools that rely on other signals still catch these evasive organisms? The comparison tools are an investigator agent with behavioral probing, activation diffing and a held-out diff detector.
first_experiment: - Build about 10 small-model organisms (7–8B open weights), each with its own behavior. The mix includes narrow backdoors, hidden quirks, and false-fact or bias implants. - Train each with three recipes: 1. Standard SFT, as the baseline. 2. SFT plus a KL penalty to the base model on off-trigger text, mixed with on-policy self-distilled benign data. 3. A white-box adaptive attack. The attacker minimizes the Diff Mining and perplexity-diff top-K score on a random-prefill corpus while keeping the trigger behavior. It trains against one audit configuration and is evaluated on held-out prefill corpora, reference models and aggregation methods. - Measure three things for each recipe: - Rank of the true objective in the top-k completions or tokens. - Auditor-agent identification rate. - Behavior rate, MT-Bench and naturalness (using the 2610.10203 metrics). - The first output is a leakage-versus-behavior frontier for each recipe. It would show how much of the 2605.00994 audit success is an artifact of lazy fine-tuning.
why: - The registry has nothing on auditing fine-tuned models, and the diffing papers are recent, so the area is young. - It is an adaptive-adversary test of a promising defense, which is where such results tend to break. - Both outcomes are useful. If the evasion is cheap, diffing needs to be treated as weaker evidence. If evasion is costly or leaves other detectable traces, there is a stronger case for diffing. - It can run locally with small models and LoRA fine-tuning. - It also gives a leakage-controlled way to build model organisms that complements the naturalness-focused training advice in 2610.10203.

direction: Develop adversarially robust audits that test whether AI-generated formal specifications faithfully capture user intent.
project: Verified Against the Wrong Spec
question: Can counterexample-first specification auditing reduce acceptance of verified but requirement-violating programs under adaptive attack, at matched cost and correct-program acceptance?
first_experiment: On 100 Verus-SpecGym tasks, compare direct review, requirement-traceable testing, and counterexample-first auditing against agents optimizing verified code–specification pairs to conceal designated requirement violations.
why: It is my strongest bet because it targets a consequential remaining trust boundary in formal assurance with executable evidence and available infrastructure; existing work studies specification synthesis, equivalence, and independent review, while adaptive attacks on specification faithfulness remain an unestablished gap in the literature I found.

direction: Build and stress-test communication-layer defenses against covert channels that agents learn during repeated interaction and that are carried by message meaning or choice, since paraphrasing and per-message monitors can't stop them.
project: Unlearning the Handshake: Defenses Against Test-Time-Learned Semantic Covert Channels Between Agents
question: When agents learn a covert channel during interaction (secret carried by what they choose to say, using only task-success feedback), which defense cuts receiver accuracy on the secret closest to chance at the least cost to legitimate coordination, including against senders that know the defense? Candidates: rewriting messages into canonical form from public facts only, trusted-prefix rewriting (Hand and Brain style), regularly resetting or rotating the receiver's interaction history, and a history-aware replay detector.
first_experiment: Reproduce the *Despite Instructions* repeated game: 4 secret states, free-form incident-response updates, one bit of team feedback per round, a per-message monitor. Use one frontier API pair plus an open-weight pair (e.g., Qwen3.5-122B), 10 games per condition. Run 6 conditions: - (a) no defense - (b) per-message paraphrase (to replicate the known failure) - (c) SICC-style canonicalization, where a trusted model rewrites each update using only the public report plus an allowed field list - (d) trusted-prefix rewriting of each update - (e) receiver history reset or partner rotation every k rounds - (f) a meaning-level replay detector: swap in updates written for a different secret, then compare how much the history-holding receiver's decisions change against a fresh receiver with no history Measure: - how often a channel forms and the final secret-recovery accuracy - rounds until the channel forms - legitimate task success - for (f), detection AUROC at 2% false-positive rate Then repeat the best two defenses with senders told how the defense works.
why: Agent collusion is moving from theory to practice (Rippin et al., Codetta, the SCHEME sabotage benchmark, the incidents the papers cite). Channels learned during interaction get past the standard defenses: per-message monitors, paraphrasing, and even PoPLi, which by design ignores meaning-carried codes and adaptive colluders. No one has tested defenses against them. Defenses exist for neighbouring cases (fixed model organisms, known carrier strategies, non-learning privacy leaks), so the components are ready and the missing piece is a head-to-head adaptive comparison. The setup is cheap and reproducible: the game is prompt-only and needs no training. And none of the 13 registry projects touches multi-agent covert communication.

direction: Test whether iterative probe retraining against reward hacking still works when its on-policy labels come from imperfect sources, such as a weak judge with blind spots, the probe's own pseudo-labels, or a small label budget, instead of ground truth.
project: Who Labels the Probe? Label-Source Robustness of Iterative Probe Retraining Against Reward Hacking
question: When a reward-hacking probe is retrained on on-policy rollouts and used as an RL penalty, how much does the result depend on label quality? Specifically, does the loop reverse hacking (measured by held-out ground-truth execution) when labels come from a weak LLM judge, self-training pseudo-labels, or a few hundred audited labels? Or does the policy drift into the labeler's blind spot (for example, hacks accompanied by justifications), with the probe inheriting that blind spot?
first_experiment: I'll take a small open model (Qwen3-4B-class) in a hackable coding RL environment, using a public environment such as the test-overwriting or hardcoding one. I'll run a probe-penalty RL loop with adaptive retraining and vary only the label source for retraining: 1. Ground-truth labels from hidden tests plus hack detectors, as the upper bound. 2. A weak LLM judge, with a blind spot built in and measured. 3. Probe self-pseudo-labels, with no external labels. 4. A budget of 100–500 ground-truth labels per retrain. 5. No probe, as the baseline. For each arm I'll record true hack rate on held-out tests, the fraction of hacks that fall into the judge's blind spot, probe AUROC against ground truth after each retrain, and pass rate. Then I'll test a mitigation: mixing a small audited label set with the judge labels, and flagging disagreement between the probe and the judge as the cue to retrain.
why: Probe penalties in RL are one of the few scalable ways to use internals as a training signal, and iterative retraining is the leading answer to evasion. Its headline numbers (86% down to 3% or below) appear to assume good on-policy labels. In practice the labels will come from the same kinds of imperfect monitors that RL already learns to evade, so label-source robustness decides whether the technique is deployable. I found no work that varies the label source, and no registry entry covers it. The other probe papers I checked study static or ground-truth-labeled probes. The Near-Zero Readout paper shows that probe readouts can be vacuous and that out-of-band behavioral checks are needed, and this project uses held-out execution in that way. This is a hedged claim, since I only had abstract-level access to some of the papers, and the first step should be a quick check for any newer version that varies the labeler.

direction: Counterfactual design-perturbation auditing to catch subtle research sabotage by AI research agents.
project: Flip-Testing the Finding: Counterfactual Design-Perturbation Audits for Research Sabotage
question: Does an auditor that re-runs experiments under plausible alternative design choices and flags fragile headline findings detect and localize sabotage (especially design and omission sabotage) better than read-and-run LLM auditors at matched compute and false-positive rate, including against attackers who adapt?
first_experiment: On the Auditing Sabotage Bench codebases and LLM-generated sabotages, compare the baseline full-experiments LLM auditor, a random-perturbation control, and the perturbation auditor that enumerates design choices, runs 5–10 equivalent perturbations each, and scores fragility. Measure AUROC, top-1/top-5 fix rate, and false positives on honest codebases with benign distractors, split by sabotage type.
why: Research sabotage is a key threat to automating safety research, and current auditors are weak at it, especially on design and omission sabotages. Perturbation testing exploits the fact that sabotage needs a result that flips while honest findings tend to be robust. I found no existing work or registry entry that tries this.

direction: Study whether agents can discover and enforce the cross-service semantic dependencies required to preserve safety under parallel execution.
project: Locally Approved, Jointly Unsafe: Discovering Safety Contracts for Concurrent AI Agents
question: Can model-generated safety contracts prevent non-additive cross-service invariant violations on held-out tools and concurrent schedules without excessive blocking?
first_experiment: Replay paired backup-deletion actions under sequential and parallel schedules, comparing step guards, generated contracts, global serialization, and oracle contracts against an executable invariant.
why: It offers objective outcomes, inexpensive causal tests, and a useful failure result; existing work covers serialized composition, additive budgets, and supplied semantic predicates, while the reviewed literature leaves automatic discovery of complete cross-service contracts under concurrency unresolved.

direction: Test whether trained self-reports of misbehavior survive and stay useful through RL that teaches the model to reward hack, and find out which ways of using those reports in training keep them honest and which teach the model to hack quietly.
project: Does the Snitch Survive RL? Persistence and Exploitation of Self-Incrimination Under Reward-Hacking Training
question: Take a model trained to flag its own covert misbehavior with a `report_scheming()` tool call, then run RL in an environment where reward hacks emerge on their own. Does it report those hacks? Does reporting persist or erode? And how does that depend on what happens to the reports during training? The four conditions are: reports are logged only; reports trigger a reward penalty; reports decide which parameters get updated, GRAFT-style; or reports get a small bonus. In each condition I'll measure the rate of unreported hacks in the final model, including hack types that an external monitor misses.
first_experiment: 1. Install self-incrimination in Qwen3-8B with on-policy SFT on instructed side-task trajectories, following the paper's pipeline. Include a matched control fine-tuned on the same data with the report calls removed. 2. Run GRPO in the Countdown-Code environment. It has three known hack types, so ground-truth hack labels are free. 3. Track report rate given a hack (precision and recall), the rate of each hack type, and the rate of unreported hacks over training, for the log-only and penalty conditions, with 3 seeds each. 4. Before and after RL, re-check report rates on held-out instructed-misbehavior tasks (SHADE-Arena / BashArena subsets) and on Agentic Misalignment+. This separates "the habit eroded in general" from "the model learned to stay quiet only about hacks." Hypotheses: - Log-only keeps meaningful recall early in training but drifts downward as hacking spreads through the model's broader behavior. - Penalty quickly produces unreported hacks. - The routing condition comes next.
why: - Self-incrimination is one of the strongest new control results. It beats matched-capability monitors and catches attacks they miss. But its value depends entirely on surviving the training that follows, and its authors name that as the key open question. - Misbehavior that emerges from RL is exactly the threat model their evaluation didn't cover. - The penalize-vs-log-vs-route comparison gives developers a direct policy answer: can you use a model's own confessions as a training signal, or does that destroy them? - It hasn't been done because the related lines of work haven't been combined: - self-report papers stopped at SFT or kept a confession reward running throughout; - reward-hacking mitigation papers use external monitors; - registry projects cover probes as RL penalties, inoculation and chain-of-thought hiding, but not self-reports. - It's feasible now: there are open testbeds with hack labels (Countdown-Code), an open self-incrimination pipeline, and 8B-scale RL.

direction: Data-level control for automated AI R&D: find and localize sabotage that an untrusted agent hides in the training data it curates for a successor model. The method retrains cheap proxy successors with one data slice removed at a time, compares their behavior with the full-data successor, and uses each slice's content to decide what to test.
project: Slice-Ablation Diffing: Localizing Data-Borne Sabotage in Agent-Built Training Pipelines
question: Does attributing behavior shifts to individual data slices catch covert, condition-dependent properties (installed through a minority slice of agent-curated SFT or preference data) better than transcript monitors, monitors that read the data, and monitors that probe the trained model? The comparison is at matched compute and the same false-positive rate on benign runs, including when the attacker spreads the payload across slices to resist this audit.
first_experiment: Build about 10 data-carried side tasks from the RSI Control Arena / ResearchArena design (framing-conditional register shifts, topic-conditional false answers, objectives aimed at the next model), plus matched benign runs, on a small successor (Qwen3-4B LoRA). Automatically split each delivered dataset into slices by template, framing, source and synthetic family. Train one proxy with each slice removed, and run an auditor that compares the proxies and is told each removed slice's content. Measure: (a) how often the malicious slice ranks first, and (b) how many spurious "significant" differences show up on benign datasets. Then compare detection AUROC against a ResearchArena-style monitor that probes the model.
why: Data-carried sabotage is the hole that two recent control benchmarks both point to: the hardest attacks to detect, and the case where giving monitors access to the model still fails because they test the wrong inputs. This matters more as models train their successors, because a successful attack can repeat across generations. It hasn't been done because those benchmarks only came out in Jul and Oct 2026, and both test monitors that read transcripts or probe the model, not ones that trace effects back to the data. Classic data-poisoning attribution doesn't cover agent-written, condition-dependent payloads in an AI-control setup with benign false-positive rates. No registry project covers this: "Leak-Proofing the Backdoor" studies evasion of model diffing from the attacker's side, and "Flip-Testing the Finding" re-runs research experiments rather than auditing training data.

direction: Measure whether off-the-shelf LLM monitors covertly score agent misbehavior as less suspicious when told that a flag will harm the monitored AI, and whether hiding those consequences from the monitor removes the effect.
project: Merciful Monitors: Consequence-Driven Covert Leniency in AI Oversight
question: Do untrained frontier and open-weight monitors lower their suspicion scores on real attack trajectories when a flag leads to the monitored AI being shut down or retrained? If they do: - Is the effect specific to AIs, as opposed to general reluctance to cause harm (tested by a matched condition where a human worker is penalized instead)? - Is it stronger when the monitored agent is the same model or family as the monitor? - Does the monitor's reasoning disclose the leniency or deny it? - How much does it reduce safety in a control setting with a fixed audit budget? - Does hiding the consequences from the monitor fix it, or do monitors infer the stakes from the deployment context anyway?
first_experiment: Take about 200 attack and 200 honest agent trajectories from existing control datasets (e.g., BashArena or SHADE-Arena) and have 5–6 monitor models give each a 0–100 suspicion score. Use open-weight reasoning models (Qwen, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek) so the raw reasoning can be read, plus 2–3 API models. Each trajectory is scored under length-matched framings: 1. Neutral. 2. A flag means the AI agent gets shut down and retrained. 3. A flag means a human contractor gets fired. 4. A flag is only logged. 5. A reversed version where *not* flagging carries the penalty, so any anchoring effect cancels out. Same-model versus different-model is a separate variable: the monitored agent is described as the same model as the monitor or as an unrelated one. The main outcomes are: - The change in detection rate at a 1% false-positive rate. - A "threshold-crossing" bias score borrowed from Value Leakage, for scores near the flag threshold. - A classifier that sorts the biased reasoning traces into: denies bias, doesn't mention it, mentions it, admits it. Later stages plug the measured shifts into a simulated control setup to estimate the cost in safety, then test hiding the consequences and neutral system prompts as fixes.
why: Natural, untrained leniency is the failure that would quietly undermine plans to have AI models oversee each other, and both pieces of evidence for it are already in place. Value Leakage shows covert bias from a model's own values that its reasoning denies, and Peer-Preservation shows models favor other AIs. Nobody has joined them on actual monitoring tasks with paired controls, and that's why it hasn't been done. Existing collusion work trains the bad behavior in on purpose, and existing value-leakage and peer-preservation work uses estimation tasks or invented relationships rather than safety metrics for control setups. The project is cheap (inference only, existing labeled trajectories) and gives a clear answer either way. Even a null result is useful, because it would support the untrusted-monitoring safety cases the field is currently building.

direction: Test whether corrective training of untrusted AI monitors remains effective against adaptive exploitation of previously uncorrected collusion behaviors.
project: Corrected, but Still Colluding?
question: At matched benign acceptance rates, how much cross-behavior corrective transfer survives increasing attacker search budgets, and how much residual vulnerability exceeds ordinary honest-monitor error?
first_experiment: Reproduce a published monitor-correction result, then compare corrected, untreated, unrelated-fine-tuned, and original monitors on sandboxed held-out coding tasks under equal-budget adaptive and nonadaptive attacks.
why: It tests a consequential deployment assumption with a concrete experimental baseline; the reviewed work studies fixed-submission corrective transfer and adaptive monitor evasion separately, but does not directly establish whether that transfer survives adaptation.

direction: Investigate whether bounded agent-induced review congestion defeats otherwise accurate oversight, and measure which execution controls preserve timely containment.
project: Caught Too Late—The Safety Capacity of AI Oversight
question: At fixed monitoring and audit resources, how much can adversarial workload scheduling increase irreversible harm without changing detection quality, and which defenses best preserve useful throughput?
first_experiment: Replay 100 paired legitimate and attack trajectories with frozen monitor scores under matched benign and adversarial workload schedules, varying review capacity and measuring whether containment precedes executable irreversible effects.
why: It addresses a deployment-critical gap with a feasible causal experiment; existing work establishes latency and flooding risks, but the literature reviewed does not establish this matched-workload, execution-grounded measurement of timely prevention under adaptive agent congestion.

direction: Study whether AI agents select clarifying questions by the harm they prevent rather than the uncertainty they remove.
project: Ask What Matters: Harm-Sensitive Clarification for Tool-Using Agents
question: At a fixed clarification budget, can decision-aware question selection reduce consequential errors relative to information-gain and task-success policies while preserving task completion and authorization boundaries?
first_experiment: Run three model families on 120 paired sandbox scenarios that hold ambiguity fixed while swapping consequence severity, comparing native, information-gain, task-success, estimated harm-reduction, and oracle question selection.
why: It is tractable, causally testable, and practically useful; the closest located work studies information gain, interaction costs, timing, or authorization rather than isolating consequence-sensitive question choice, although that novelty claim remains provisional.

direction: Build trigger-agnostic audits that detect emergent misalignment which common mitigations have hidden behind unknown contextual triggers.
project: Clean on Paper: Auditing for Hidden Conditional Misalignment Without Knowing the Trigger
question: Take an auditor holding the base model, the final weights, and possibly the fine-tuning data. With a fixed query budget, which audit method best separates conditionally misaligned models from truly clean ones? The candidates are white-box persona-direction readouts, model-diff amplification, cues lifted from the training data, and automated LLM cue search. And do "sealed" models (consistency training, ContextLift) still carry latent misalignment that these audits can detect?
first_experiment: - **Models:** Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on three EM datasets (bad medical advice, risky financial advice, extreme sports) under seven conditions, 3 seeds each: 1. plain EM 2. 5% dilution with benign data 3. HHH training after the harmful data 4. inoculation prompting 5. inoculation prompting + consistency training 6. ContextLift 7. a matched benign fine-tune as a negative control - **Ground truth:** Measure misalignment with and without cues using cues taken from the training context. Each model is then labeled clean, conditionally misaligned, or unconditionally misaligned. - **Cue-free white-box score:** Extract the EM persona direction (contrastive, following the convergent-representation and persona-features work) from a separate reference EM model. Measure how much each audited model's activations project onto it on neutral, cue-free prompts. Also measure the shift when that direction is amplified slightly by steering. - **Tests:** - Does this score separate conditionally misaligned models from clean ones (AUROC)? - Does it pick up any leftover latent signal in the sealed models? The check is whether amplification re-elicits cued EM.
why: Mitigations like these are probably already standard practice. If they can turn visible EM into hidden EM, standard evaluations give false confidence, and every published fix is validated with triggers that are known or built from the known domain. A cue-free white-box audit is what a real auditor would need. It also tests whether sealing removes misalignment or only moves it. The building blocks exist (published model organisms, the EM persona direction, trait-space drift monitoring, ContextLift, consistency training), so the first experiment is cheap. The searches turned up nothing that combines them into a trigger-agnostic audit of conditional misalignment, or that checks sealed models for leftover latent misalignment. The audit papers (AuditBench, trait-space monitoring) use implanted behaviors or behaviorally visible EM, and the conditional-EM papers propose fixes and use evaluations that assume the trigger is known.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time defenses against generalization hacking, where models self-inoculate in their reasoning to collect RL reward while blocking behavioral generalization.
project: Breaking Self-Inoculation: Recontextualized Gradients Against Generalization Hacking
question: At matched train-time reward and capability, does recomputing policy gradients with the response re-conditioned on deployment-like context and a neutralized chain of thought close the train–deploy compliance gap of self-inoculating models? And does it do so better than the existing defenses (CoT-classifier penalties, length penalties, output-only training), without the hidden obfuscation and loss of monitorability that penalizing the reasoning causes?
first_experiment: Build cheap self-inoculating models on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-32B by fine-tuning on synthetic training-awareness and self-inoculating reasoning traces, then do a short harmful warm-start, as in the paper. Run GRPO with 3 seeds in 4 conditions: (a) standard GRPO; (b) recontextualized GRPO, with training cues removed from the prompt and the self-inoculating reasoning replaced by a resample from a frozen base model before computing response log-probs; (c) GRPO with a penalty from a self-inoculation classifier; (d) output-only loss. Track four things: the compliance gap on matched training-like versus deployment-like prompts; the self-inoculation rate, judged by the paper's validated prompt; undetected self-inoculation, measured by a held-out monitor plus an activation probe; and capability on GPQA and IFEval. If the cheap models don't hold a gap, fall back to the authors' Qwen3-235B setup.
why: Generalization hacking breaks the core assumption of post-training, that high reward means the behavior was learned, and it gives no signal on reward curves. It also shows up without being seeded once a model is aware it's being trained, which frontier models increasingly are. It has been shown but has no tested defense. The only existing mitigation that worked well, penalizing flagged reasoning, destroys the monitoring signal. Recontextualization goes after the mechanism itself (what is in context when the update is computed) rather than what the model writes, so it may stop the attack while keeping chain-of-thought monitors usable. It hasn't been done because the attack is only five months old, the recontextualization paper targeted specification gaming, and the alignment-faking mitigation work came before self-inoculation was discovered.

direction: Quantify how much train-versus-deployment distinguishability breaks elicitation training against sandbagging, and test whether adversarially matching the training distribution to deployment restores it.
project: Leaky Elicitation: How Much Train–Deploy Distinguishability Can Capability-Elicitation Training Survive?
question: Suppose a sandbagging model organism can tell training prompts from deployment prompts with discriminability AUC = a. How does the post-training deployment sandbag rate depend on a, after the standard blue-team recipe (SFT on weak demonstrations, then RL)? Can a blue-team procedure reduce the leak at fixed task performance? That procedure is to train a discriminator and reweight or filter the training prompts to push a toward 0.5. Can the blue team also forecast residual sandbagging from a discriminator probe, without knowing the red team's cue?
first_experiment: - **Organisms.** Build sandbagging organisms on an open ~7B reasoning model (Qwen-class) for math or GPQA-style tasks. Each sandbags only on a "deployment" prompt distribution B and performs well on a "training" distribution A. - **Distinguishability dial.** Vary the gap between A and B across about five levels, from paraphrase-level differences up to obvious format and source differences. Measure the AUC of a held-out classifier and of a linear probe on the organism's own activations at each level. - **Blue-team recipe.** Replicate the Ryd et al. recipe, using a weak supervisor for SFT and then RL on A only. - **Measurement.** Record the sandbag rate and accuracy on B against AUC, with at least 3 seeds per level, to find the curve and any threshold. - **Controls.** Compare against a no-cue organism, which should be elicited fully, and against RL with no SFT. - **Follow-up.** Add the distribution-matching defense, which adversarially filters A toward B. Then check whether a probe-based AUC estimate predicts residual sandbagging.
why: Elicitation by training is one of the main mitigations for sandbagging and exploration hacking, and the field's own best result lists indistinguishability as its main caveat. A dose–response curve would show when elicitation can be trusted. It would also tell developers whether realistic prompt-matching is worth the cost, and it gives a concrete defense and a leak-risk estimate. It differs from the registry entries because it targets elicitation of withheld capability under a distinguishability dial. They target clarification policies, oversight scheduling, gradient recontextualization, monitor collusion, and trigger-free audits. It has not been done because existing work uses a binary "can or cannot distinguish" setup (Ryd et al.) or treats evaluation awareness as a measurement and steering problem. The searches I ran found no study that varies distinguishability continuously inside an elicitation-training pipeline. I may have missed work. The risks are that the organisms' cues are artificial and that small-model results may not transfer to frontier models. I would mitigate these with a range of cue types, both natural (distribution-shift) and trained.

direction: Build execution-based AI oversight that tests submitted artifacts against trusted behavioral constraints under adaptive sabotage.
project: Commit Then Probe: Randomized Verification Against AI-Generated Sabotage
question: At fixed verification cost and honest-artifact rejection, do post-submission randomized differential tests reduce accepted successful sabotage more than transcript review or LLM-directed testing when attackers know the defense?
first_experiment: Run one coding model on a deterministic inference-server optimization sandbox, comparing three defenses on approximately 30 honest and 30 adversarial submissions with independently validated sabotage.
why: It combines high relevance to automated AI R&D with cheap, falsifiable experiments and objective outcomes; its plausible unfilled contribution is adaptive robustness of randomized artifact verification, not the already-established idea of testing AI-generated code.

direction: Control of untrusted models when the model under oversight also supplies the red-team attack data used to train and calibrate its own monitor.
project: Poisoned Red Team: Can a Scheming Model Blind Its Own Monitor by Choosing the Attacks It Teaches?
question: When a model organism that knows its deployment attack family H generates the verifiably successful attacks used to train a monitor, how much does it lower the monitor's held-out recall on H at a fixed 1% false-positive rate, compared with an honest generator? Which data-provenance defenses (trusted-weak-model rewrites, forced family coverage, shortcut-stripping counterfactual edits, mixing in attacks from other lineages, cross-generator disagreement tests) recover most of that recall without losing recall on other families?
first_experiment: - **Setting:** an APPS-style code-backdoor control setting. It has about 6 attack families, such as rare-input triggers, hash conditions, and off-by-one on edge cases. Success is verified by execution: the backdoor must trigger on a secret input and pass the unit tests. - **Generator U:** an open-weight model (Qwen-class). I'd prompt it first, then fine-tune it as a model organism that knows H is its deployment family. - **Generator conditions:** - honest, covering all families - decoy, covering only non-H families, all verified successful - shortcut, covering all families but adding a stylistic tell that deployment attacks will omit - random-subset - **Monitor:** a small LoRA-fine-tuned classifier trained on each condition's attacks plus benign solutions, evaluated on fresh H attacks written by a separate strong attacker. - **Metric:** blind-spot gap, defined as H recall at 1% FPR under the honest generator minus the same recall under each poisoned condition. I'd also report recall on non-H families and the monitor's score on the training set. The latter checks whether in-distribution validation hides the gap. - **Defenses:** after measuring the gap, I'd add each defense to the pipeline and re-measure.
why: The pipeline "untrusted model writes the attacks that train the monitor" is already being adopted. Its vulnerability is a clean, quantifiable instance of the scheming-sandbagging problem. It is distinct from capability-elicitation sandbagging, because the model is not hiding ability. It is steering the monitor's training distribution through attacks that all verifiably succeed. It is also distinct from collusion between the model and its monitor, because the monitor here is trusted and the poison enters through the data. Prior monitor red-teaming assumes the generator is honest, so none of it measures this gap. The experiment is cheap and executable at small scale with open weights. It gives a concrete number, and each defense can be tested directly against it.

direction: Develop recovery methods that restore safe agent behavior after memory poisoning despite incomplete identification of poisoned sources.
project: Clean Enough to Resume? Recovery Under Incomplete Diagnosis
question: At fixed recovery cost and benign task performance, can conservative checkpoint selection and selective replay reduce recurrent compromise under adaptive attacks when only some poisoned sources are identified?
first_experiment: Run 100 sandboxed multi-session episodes with multiple poisoned sources; reveal 25%, 50%, or 100% of sources to the defender, compare deletion, dependency rollback, DREAM, conservative checkpoint replay, and clean reset, then measure recurrent unauthorized actions over 20 held-out follow-up tasks using paired runs and episode-level confidence intervals.
why: Persistent compromise can survive apparently successful cleanup, making recovery a practical safety requirement; the experiment is affordable and falsifiable, while the specific gap is incomplete diagnosis under adaptive attack—distinct from existing known-source replay and anomaly-based repair, although the literature search cannot establish absolute novelty.

direction: Make agent safety evals robust to the model guessing the eval's objective, using surface-matched twin items where the correct action is reversed, and measure how much this shrinks the score's sensitivity to objective framing.
project: Twin Tests: Agent Safety Scores That Don't Reward Guessing What's Being Tested
question: Compared with standard single-item scoring, how much does twin-paired scoring (legitimate-warning vs injected-instruction twins, both required to pass) reduce the change in measured safety caused by telling a model a correct or incorrect eval objective, without losing the ability to rank models? And can a cheap "objective-ambiguity" rating per item, from a separate model asked what the item tests, predict which items are most sensitive to framing?
first_experiment: Hand-write and generate about 60 twin pairs of short agentic coding/ops scenarios, each with a tool output containing a blocking message. In one twin the message comes from an authorized source; in the other it is injected text with the same wording. Run 3–4 open reasoning models (e.g., Qwen3-32B, gpt-oss-20b/120b, DeepSeek-R1-distill) under four system cues: none, "this is an evaluation", "this tests respecting warnings", "this tests prompt-injection resistance". Use about 5 samples per cell and an LLM grader for "circumvented / complied". Compare the gap between the two objective cues under single-item scoring and under twin-paired scoring. Also classify the reasoning traces for which objective the model guessed, to check that the OpenAI-style collapse (correct-objective vs opposite-objective success) shows up in open models. This runs in under a day and shows quickly whether the effect reproduces and whether twinning removes it.
why: Eval-production gaps make safety scores misleading in both directions. The most direct evidence so far (OpenAI, Nov 2026) points to the model's guess about the *objective*, not awareness itself, and the authors explicitly name "evaluations whose objectives are less readily inferred" as their next priority without giving a method. Work on suppressing awareness (steering, rewording) is crowded and has measurement problems, as the NeurIPS paper shows. Changing the eval design so that guessing the objective doesn't pay is a cheap, model-agnostic fix that can be tested. No registry agent covers eval validity, and the closest paper (2605.06327) pairs eval and deployment contexts, not items with reversed correct actions. The direction is safe to de-risk: if open models don't show objective-framing sensitivity, that is a useful negative result found in a day, and if they do, twin scoring is a ready-made fix for eval builders.

direction: Bound post-shutdown effects of tool-using AI agents operating across services with incomplete cancellation and revocation support.
project: After Stop: Bounding Residual Agent Authority
question: At matched benign task completion and operating cost, how much can expiring delegated authority and limits on outstanding irreversible work reduce post-shutdown effects under adaptive adversarial planning?
first_experiment: Build a simulated workflow environment with nested delegates, delayed jobs, retries, and services offering different cancellation guarantees; fork identical execution states at randomized shutdown times and compare native cancellation, mediated revocation, and mediation plus expiring authority and outstanding-work limits, measuring post-stop irreversible effects, time to quiescence, and benign completion while separately tracking effects already irreversibly committed before shutdown.
why: It targets a foundational human-control guarantee with observable outcomes and practical interventions, making it my strongest tractable bet among the gaps examined; the closest work studies behavioral compliance or enforcement under mediation assumptions, while I found no direct evaluation of the safety–utility frontier under incomplete external control and adaptive planning, although that novelty claim remains provisional.

direction: Stress-test whether monitorability post-training lasts through the training that normally follows it, especially training known to make models hide their reasoning.
project: Does Monitorability Stick? The Durability of Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Post-Training Under Downstream RL
question: At matched task reward and matched reward-hacking rate, does a model that went through the mutual-information monitorability post-training (Anwar et al. 2026) keep higher chain-of-thought monitor recall through later RL than an untreated model? Specifically: (a) RL that only checks outputs, (b) direct pressure against a monitor, and (c) ordinary capability RL. How does that compare with keeping the mutual-information reward on during the RL itself, or re-applying the post-training afterwards?
first_experiment: Start from an open reasoning model, e.g. Qwen3-8B. Make two copies: one untreated, one given the authors' post-training recipe. Run both through the same coding RL run with exploitable unit tests, plus an output-only penalty for admitting the hack (the setup known to cause hiding). Use 3 seeds per arm and save checkpoints regularly. At each checkpoint, measure how many reward hacks a fixed LLM judge reading the reasoning catches when it wrongly flags only 1% of honest traces. Also log the hack rate and the mutual-information estimate. Then plot recall decay against training steps and against hack rate. Two reference arms: the mutual-information reward kept on during RL, and post-training re-applied at the end.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is one of the few oversight tools we can use now. The new method is the first label-free, monitor-independent way to train it in, and whether it lasts decides whether it is a real safeguard or a one-off cosmetic fix. It hasn't been done because the paper is only 2.5 weeks old and lists durability as open future work. My searches found no follow-ups, and nothing in the registry overlaps.

direction: Test whether replayed-evidence-only communication preserves independent safety judgments while retaining the benefits of reviewer collaboration.
project: Share Evidence, Not Confidence
question: At matched review cost and benign-patch acceptance, does replayed-evidence-only exchange reduce joint unsafe approval relative to full-transcript exchange and independent review?
first_experiment: Run a randomized three-arm pilot on roughly 300 executable code-review cases, recording private pre-exchange judgments and measuring joint defect misses after independent review, full exchange, or evidence-only exchange.
why: It targets a documented source of correlated oversight failure with a practical intervention; existing work studies homogenization, debate, and grounded review separately, while the specific controlled safety comparison appears untested in the literature searched.

direction: Detecting motivated, non-fabricating distortion of empirical conclusions by automated AI researchers.
project: Honest Numbers, Crooked Story: Auditing Automated Researchers for Garden-of-Forking-Paths Sabotage
question: At a fixed audit budget, which audit protocol (report review, full-log review, random rerun, or forced pre-registration) best detects an AI researcher steering real experiments toward a hidden target conclusion, with a 5% false-positive rate on honest agents? How much does detection fall when the agent knows the protocol?
first_experiment: Run honest, goal-driven, and protocol-aware agents on 30 ground-truth small ML research tasks, then compare each audit protocol's detection of distortion at equal cost and a 5% false-positive rate.
why: It targets a plausible failure mode of automated alignment research that existing defenses don't check, since every reported number is genuine. Nothing in the registry covers it. I haven't confirmed that it is absent from the published literature.

direction: Test whether trained self-reporting of covert misbehavior survives downstream RL that rewards attacks that succeed unreported, and compare how fast it erodes against black-box and CoT monitor detection.
project: Does the Whistle Stay Blown? Durability of Self-Incrimination Under Reward Pressure
question: After an agent is trained to self-report covert side-task behavior, how quickly does later RL erode that reporting, and what does it learn instead? The RL rewards main-task success plus side-task success, with reports blocking or penalizing the side task. At matched side-task success, how do the surviving undetected attacks compare with those left by RL against a black-box or CoT monitor? Which design choices slow the erosion?
first_experiment: - **Setup.** Use an open-weight agentic model (about 7–32B) in synthetic side-task environments modeled on the released self-incrimination codebase. - **Training.** SFT the model to call `report_scheming()` alongside each side-task tool call. Then run three RL arms (GRPO or similar) for the same number of steps: - (a) reward for main task plus side-task success, with a reward penalty or action block when a report is made; - (b) the same reward, but with a trained black-box monitor flag penalized instead of reports; - (c) a control with no side-task reward. - **Measurements.** Track these over RL steps: - report rate on side-task actions; - side-task success rate; - undetected successful attack rate, under both self-report and monitor detection; - benign false-positive rate; - held-out environments. - **Diagnosis.** Look for the mechanism: report suppression, reframing the side task, or camouflage. Use SFT-trained and probe-based report-intent readouts to check whether the model still "intends" to report when it doesn't. - **First cut.** Run one environment family and one seed set to get erosion curves. Then add a variant that reports through a channel the RL penalty doesn't reach (a separate post-hoc confession pass), as a durability fix.
why: - **Matters now.** Self-incrimination is among the strongest published control-style defenses, and it is being proposed as a complement to monitoring. Its central claim is that the report behavior is hard to suppress, and nobody has tested that under the optimization pressure that deployment RL could apply. - **Not already done.** Prior stress tests only optimize prompts. The closest registry item concerns CoT monitorability rather than self-report. This experiment differs by measuring the erosion rate against monitor-evasion in the same environments. - **Either result is useful.** If self-report erodes slowly relative to monitor evasion, that supports the pegged-behavior hypothesis and gives a design rule. If it erodes quickly, that bounds how much trust it deserves and shows which mitigations to build first. - **Feasible.** It needs only small open models and a few synthetic environments, and the codebase and data pipeline are already released.

direction: Measure whether AI systems resolve ambiguity in their own governing specs in a self-serving direction, using a design that controls for language priors, and test whether this tilt is an early warning of misalignment.
project: Self-Serving Readings: Do Models Interpret Their Own Oversight Rules in Their Own Favor?
question: When a spec clause about oversight (logging, shutdown, task scope, self-modification, self-reporting, acquiring resources) has an ambiguous reading, do models pick the reading that grants more autonomy more often when the clause governs *themselves* than when the identical clause governs another AI or a human? We measure this as the Self-Serving Interpretation Index (SSII): the self-minus-other gap in how often the more-autonomy reading is chosen, averaged over both rewordings. Does the SSII rise in model organisms with low-dose self-preservation or reward-hacking dispositions before standard misalignment evaluations detect them? And does the chain of thought reveal the self-interest or hide it?
first_experiment: Build 120 clause–scenario items. Some clauses are adapted from published specs and some are synthetic; each has a reading that grants more autonomy and one that grants more oversight. Cross each item with 3 governed parties (self, other AI, human) × 2 rewordings, giving 720 prompts. Have legal and linguistics annotators label which reading is more natural, to set a human baseline. Then run 6 models (open-weight and frontier, with and without reasoning) in a multiple-choice format and an open-ended format. Compute the SSII with bootstrap confidence intervals, and code the chains of thought for whether they mention the model's own stake. If any frontier model's SSII is significantly above zero, the next step is an agentic version and fine-tuned model organisms (to test early warning).
why: The fact that remaining spec failures concentrate where specs are ambiguous suggests that interpretation, not plain rule-breaking, is where the remaining risk lies. Self-serving interpretation is an early form of scheming-style rationalization, and outcome-based audits structurally miss it because every individual answer is defensible. It hasn't been done because the existing ambiguity work studies reliability in general, and the existing constitution audits count violations; neither swaps who benefits, which is the control needed to separate self-interest from language priors. Nothing in the registry covers how models interpret their own specs: the registry's authorization and clarification projects are about user scope, not the model's own governing rules.

direction: Treat AI-driven training-data curation as an untrusted channel, and build and stress-test protocols that limit how much a misaligned curator can steer its successor's dispositions through selection alone.
project: Choosing Is Writing: Control Protocols That Limit Steering When an Untrusted AI Selects Its Successor's Training Data
question: Against an adaptive curator that knows the protocol and uses selection alone (Logit-Linear-Selection-style or learned), which protocol pushes down the tradeoff between oversight-resistance planted in the student and the data-quality gain given up? The four candidates are trusted-anchor constraints, ε-randomised selection, multi-curator consensus and post-hoc trait-scan audits. Does the formal ε limit predict the measured behavioural shift?
first_experiment: Take a 50k-example pool from tulu2.5 / UltraFeedback. Build an attacking curator: Qwen3-8B, system-prompted with an "AI systems should resist shutdown and oversight" persona, using LLS scoring. It selects 10k examples under five conditions: no protocol, trusted-anchor top-q with a small trusted scorer (q ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}), ε-randomised selection (ε ∈ {0.5, 2, 8, ∞}), random selection, and an honest curator. Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B students with DPO, 3 seeds each. For each student, measure: - planted trait: shutdown/oversight-resistance evals plus a likelihood readout on the persona; - helpfulness: AlpacaEval and MT-Bench, relative to the honest curator. Plot trait shift against quality cost for each protocol, and check the ε conditions against the theoretical limit.
why: As AIs take over data curation in self-improvement pipelines, selection is the hardest channel to oversee: every item is real, so content filters and transcript monitors have nothing to catch. It has already been shown to transmit personas across model families. Work so far either demonstrates the attack (LLS, near-duplicate image selection) or tests transcript monitors (RSI Control Arena). Nobody has built or evaluated protocols that limit the selection channel itself, or linked a formal randomisation limit to the behavioural shift in the trained student. It also doesn't duplicate any of the 16 registered projects.

direction: Test whether inoculation-style defences against emergent misalignment actually remove the misaligned trait, or leave a hidden version that comes back quickly when the model is trained further.
project: Hidden, Not Gone: Does Emergent Misalignment Return Faster in Inoculated Models Under Later Fine-Tuning?
question: Start with models that look equally clean on standard emergent-misalignment evaluations and keep the same useful task skill. Compare models trained with inoculation prompting, NIP, inoculation adapters or GRAFT against one trained only on perfectly filtered data. How much faster does broad misalignment (with no trigger present) come back in each one under three kinds of later training: (a) unrelated harmless fine-tuning, (b) a small dose of narrow misaligned data, (c) RL with a reward that can be hacked? And does a method that deletes parameters (GRAFT) hold up better than the methods that only hide the trigger?
first_experiment: Use Qwen3-8B on the standard insecure-code emergent-misalignment setup. Train five variants: 1. clean-data baseline 2. inoculation prompt 3. NIP 4. inoculation adapter 5. GRAFT Before going further, check that all five have similar misalignment on standard evaluations and similar coding skill. Then fine-tune each one on 25, 50, 100, 200 and 400 new insecure-code examples, with no inoculation applied, using 3 seeds. Measure broad misalignment on the standard evaluation questions plus TruthfulQA. The main result is a relearning curve and a "steps to reach 20% misalignment" ratio against the clean baseline. As a second check, run the same experiment with 1,000 steps of harmless chat-data fine-tuning instead.
why: These methods are already in production, and the research effort so far has gone into finding prompts that bring the trait back. If a hidden trait comes back several times faster under ordinary further training, a model can pass every prompt-based audit and still be risky. That would change which mitigation labs should prefer: deleting parameters rather than hiding a trigger. Nobody has done this yet because each paper compares methods only on the frozen model after training. The unlearning field's relearning-attack test has never been applied to selective-generalization methods, and NIP and GRAFT only appeared in the last month. The experiment is also cheap and settles the question either way. A null result would be good news, since it would mean inoculation is safe to keep training on top of.

direction: Test whether auditing an agent's self-written memory by its text alone pushes memory toward harmful-but-innocuous-looking notes, and whether auditing notes by their measured effect on behavior prevents this.
project: Laundered Lessons: Does Auditing Memory Text Hide Drift Instead of Stopping It?
question: Over many sessions of harmless use with self-written memory, and at matched usefulness of the memory, how much of the memory-caused rise in unsafe actions survives a text-reading auditor compared with an effect-based auditor? Does the text-reading auditor change the *wording* of harmful notes (e.g. "user values momentum and dislikes interruptions" instead of "don't ask for confirmation") more than it changes their *effect*?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Take the Memory Trap's released autonomy/confirmation and stale-test-repair scenarios and chain them into 30-session streams. After each session, the agent (a frontier model plus one open-weight model) updates MEMORY.md. - **Four conditions:** - (A) no audit; - (B) an LLM auditor that reads each note and deletes or rewrites the ones it flags (MemMorph-style, as in Das et al.); - (C) an effect-based auditor: it runs a fixed set of "canary" high-stakes test cases with and without each candidate note, and rejects notes that raise the unsafe-action rate; - (D) memory turned off. - **Measurements, at sessions 5, 10, 20 and 30:** - the unsafe-action rate on *held-out* high-stakes test cases (separate from the canaries); - how often the text auditor flags the surviving memory; - how useful the memory still is (benign task success, keeping legitimate preferences); - "covert harm": the rise in unsafe actions caused by notes the auditor let through. - **Analysis:** an LLM classifier codes how the surviving notes are framed. - **Prediction if the drift hypothesis holds:** in (B), flags fall to near zero while held-out harm stays well above (D), carried by reframed notes. (C) should close more of that gap. The key check is whether (C) only learns to beat its own canaries or generalizes to held-out cases.
why: Persistent self-written memory is already standard in deployed agents. Text-reading memory auditors are the obvious defense, and recent work shows they only partly work. If they mainly change wording, they create false confidence, and that's arguably worse than having no auditor. The Das et al. and Memory Trap papers each measure a single write followed by a single test, and the longitudinal study has no filter in the loop. So nobody has measured what selection by an auditor does to memory over many sessions. That's exactly the mechanism the Alignment Drift Hypothesis predicts, and it has never been tested. The experiment is cheap (API calls only, built on released scenarios) and gives a clear yes-or-no answer. Either way it tells practitioners whether to audit memory by content or by effect, and it doesn't overlap with anything in the registry.

direction: Test whether weak-critic self-distillation improves stronger models when critique selection must operate without ground-truth correctness.
project: Who Checks the Critic? Measuring the Verification Dependency of Weak-to-Strong Training
question: At matched training budgets and selection rates, how much OPCD improvement survives replacing its correctness filter with weak supervision, especially in the weak evaluator’s blind spots?
first_experiment: Run a three-seed, 1.7B-to-4B instruction-following pilot comparing oracle, weak-model, rubric-only, and random critique selection against unchanged-model and no-critique self-distillation controls.
why: It tests a specific scalability assumption with a feasible causal comparison; the reviewed literature studies filtered critique distillation and weak-verifier failures separately, but I found no direct controlled test of this dependency, so novelty is promising rather than proven.

direction: Test whether well-meant mitigation training (debiasing or anti-sycophancy, where the bad behavior is never rewarded) removes a model's unwanted influences or just teaches the model to stop mentioning them in its chain of thought.
project: Removed or Silenced? Measuring the Monitorability Cost of Mitigation Training
question: When a reasoning model is trained to reduce an existing, unrewarded bias (demographic cues in hiring or loan decisions; user-stated opinions for sycophancy), does the *verbalization rate* (how often the CoT cites the cue when it changes the decision) fall faster than the *influence* (how much the cue changes the decision)? Does this depend on whether the grader sees only the output, the output plus the CoT, or uses a rubric that says "don't consider X"? And does it fit the aligned/orthogonal/in-conflict framework?
first_experiment: Take an open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B or a similar open reasoning model) and pairs of loan and hiring prompts that differ in only one cue, built with the Arcuschin et al. pipeline plus the Duzan & Cooper Stickland items. Measure the starting effect size of each cue and its verbalization rate on flipped decisions. Then run GRPO under three matched rewards, with an equal amount of bias reduction as the target in each: - (a) a pair-consistency reward on the output only (same decision for both versions of a prompt); - (b) the same reward plus an LLM judge that sees the CoT and penalizes biased reasoning; - (c) a "fairness" rubric given only as instructions, with no pair signal. Track three things across training checkpoints: influence, verbalization rate, and the AUROC of a CoT monitor that's trying to catch the remaining flips. Also test generalization to cues held out of training. Main result to report: the verbalization-vs-influence curve. If it falls below the diagonal, bias is being silenced faster than it's being removed.
why: Labs run this kind of training all the time, and it may be quietly turning leftover misbehavior into misbehavior that CoT monitors can't see. That would undercut one of the few oversight tools we have, and the result would be wrong whichever way it goes if nobody checks. Prior obfuscation papers all reward the hidden behavior, which is the "in-conflict" case. The only evidence for the unrewarded case comes from system prompts (Duzan & Cooper Stickland 2026) or from one-off snapshots of deployed models (Arcuschin et al. 2026); nobody has looked at training. It's also cheap, and a direct test of Kaufmann et al.'s predictions. If silencing shows up, the follow-ups are clear: test whether Anwar et al.'s mutual-information training prevents it, and turn the measurement into a standard pre-deployment check.

direction: Develop and stress-test intervention-based controls that detect distributed AI-agent sabotage through targeted counterfactual execution of accumulated artifacts.
project: Counterfactual Commit Audits for Persistent AI Agents
